citation: Mueller, M. & Wehner, R. (1988). "Path integration in desert ants, Cataglyphis fortis." PNAS 85(14), 5287-5290.

derivation.human: Integrate the commanded twist over the episode to hold a vector back to the start, and steer by THAT vector rather than by pose_estimate once the estimate is untrustworthy. Because it accumulates commanded motion rather than believed position, its error is independent of the drift injected into pose_estimate - which is what makes it a fallback rather than a second copy of the same fault.
derivation.model: Integrate a home vector from the commanded Twist stream itself — the only channel to the frozen locomotion policy — rather than from the drifting odometry pose. Maintain (r, phi): r the estimated straight-line distance back to the start, phi the bearing to start in the robot's current body frame. Per control tick of duration dt, first rotate the vector by the executed yaw, phi <- phi - wz*dt, then subtract the executed translation, updating (r, phi) from the planar displacement (vx*dt, vy*dt). This is the ant's incremental scheme: one vector, updated in place, never a stored path. Two consequences follow from the paper's actual finding — that the accumulator is approximate and its error is turn-driven. First, carry an uncertainty radius sigma that grows with accumulated absolute yaw rather than with elapsed time, since turns are what corrupt the estimate: sigma <- sigma + k_turn*|wz|*dt + k_lin*|v|*dt. Second, the home vector is a coarse heading source, not a position fix: emit it as a bearing bias into the goal-seeking Twist, and once r drops below sigma, stop trusting it and hand over to a local systematic search instead of driving to a point the accumulator claims is the origin. Every constant here (k_turn, k_lin, the r < sigma handover) is mine; the paper supplies the structure — single accumulated vector, approximate update, turn-dependent systematic error, handover when the vector is spent — not these values.

mechanism.human: Cataglyphis maintains a continuously updated vector to its nest by integrating its own outbound path, and on release runs that vector directly rather than retracing the route. The integration is independent of landmarks entirely, and it carries characteristic systematic errors rather than random ones.
mechanism.model: Cataglyphis fortis continuously accumulates a single home vector from its own locomotion — direction plus distance travelled — and steers by that vector alone when returning, without landmarks. Mueller and Wehner showed the accumulation is not exact trigonometric integration: on forced two-leg outbound paths the ants' initial homeward courses deviate from the true home direction systematically and reproducibly, as a function of the turn angle between the legs. The animal is running a cheap incremental approximation. Why this helps: the state is O(1) — one vector, updated per step, no path memory, no map — and on natural foraging paths, where turns are many and signed in both directions, the per-turn errors largely cancel, so the approximation buys enormous computational savings at negligible cost in the regime the animal actually operates in. The error is a property of the algorithm, not of noise, so it is predictable and bounded rather than random.

trigger.human: The localisation confidence proxy, pose_error_estimate, exceeds the level at which the pose estimate can still be steered by.
trigger.model: Applies whenever the robot is displacing itself and a return-to-origin or origin-relative estimate may later be needed: during any exploration leg with no disclosed goal, during any excursion around an obstacle, and at any point where the odometry pose estimate is the only thing linking current position to the start. It does NOT apply when an external position fix is available; a fix should reset the vector rather than be blended into it.

span.human: p. 5287, abstract: "This approximation is characterized by small, but systematic, navigational errors that helped us elucidate the ant's way of computing its mean home vector." Same page: "the homeward courses of the ants deviate significantly and systematically from the true homeward direction, with the error angle depending on the turning angle and the ratio a/b of the lengths of the two legs of the path", quantified in Fig. 2B. (The Greek symbols for the two angles do not survive text extraction and are described rather than quoted here.)
